front: Can you balance an equation by changing subscripts?
back: No. Only change coefficients; changing subscripts changes the substance (H₂O vs H₂O₂).

front: Writing an ionic equation for neutralisation of HCl(aq) by NaOH(aq)?
back: Split aqueous strong electrolytes into ions, cancel spectator ions (Na⁺, Cl⁻): H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s) — white precipitate; Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectators.

front: Mass of CO₂ from 10.0 g CaCO₃ (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂)?
Limiting reactant vs reactant in excess?
back: Limiting: completely used up and determines the amount of product. Excess: some remains unreacted after the reaction.

front: Amount of excess reactant left over?
back: Use the limiting reactant’s moles and the mole ratio to find moles of excess reactant used; subtract from the moles present at the start.
n(known) = cV (V in dm³) → mole ratio from equation → n(unknown) → c(unknown) = n/V (scale up if an aliquot was taken).
Add a known excess of reagent to the sample, then titrate the unreacted excess; amount reacted with sample = total added − excess. Used for insoluble or slow-reacting solids (e.g. CaCO₃).

front: Volume of H₂ at STP from 0.10 mol Mg + excess HCl?
back: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂; n(H₂) = 0.10 mol; V = 0.10 × 22.7 = 2.27 dm³.
Incomplete or reversible reaction, side reactions, loss during transfer/purification, impure reactants.
Yield: how much product is actually obtained vs theoretical (practical efficiency). Atom economy: fraction of reactant mass ending in the desired product (theoretical, from the equation).
Less waste per kg of product and fewer resources used. Addition reactions have 100% atom economy; substitution and elimination lower.
The maximum mass (or amount) of product calculated from the limiting reactant, assuming complete reaction with no losses.
